corrected_en: To nullify it. According to us, since we rule that chatichah na'asis neveilah applies to all prohibitions, and likewise regarding a prohibition attached to a piece, sixty is required against the entire piece. The same applies here: sixty is required against the entire piece to which the forbidden fat is attached, and nevertheless that piece itself remains forbidden. Shach.

Until it cools. Meaning, if he removes the piece while it is hot, the piece will become forbidden because of the fat within it, since the piece itself does not contain sixty against the fat. But when he leaves it in the pot, the absorbed taste spreads evenly throughout the entire contents. One should not object that the piece must necessarily have been salted beforehand, for otherwise it would be forbidden because of blood and the cooked food would require sixty against the entire piece; if so, it should already have become forbidden when salted together with the fat and could never again become permitted. The answer is that the case concerns fat forbidden only d'rabbanan, or the fat of a lean animal, which through salting forbids only the thickness of a peel. Alternatively, the piece originally contained sixty against the fat, and afterward, before cooking, part of the piece was cut away. End of the Shach's words.

Neveilah. If so, this piece is in any event forbidden because the prohibition is attached to it. Therefore one should remove the piece, etc., for removing it causes no loss at all, and there is no reason to leave it unnecessarily in the pot. Shach.

corrected_en: Beforehand. The same applies if the child reached eight days old but was not circumcised during his lifetime for some reason. Shach. If an infant was buried within eight days without circumcision with a flint, it is permitted to exhume him and circumcise him with a flint. Responsa Knesses Yechezkel, question 44.

For conversion. The Taz writes: It appears to me that the reason is that we say that Avraham Avinu stands and identifies one who is circumcised and does not allow him to enter Gehinnom. One who circumcises a non-Jew thereby weakens the identifying sign of circumcision that distinguishes Israel. End of his words. The Shach, however, explains that the case concerns circumcision for medical purposes, such as where the non-Jew needs his foreskin removed because of an injury or the like. It is forbidden to heal him without payment, but for payment it is permitted. See there.

corrected_en: How, etc. In chapter 9 of Hilchos Melachim, Rambam writes that six forbidden relations apply to a ben Noach: his mother, his father's wife, a married woman, his maternal sister, a male, and an animal. This is derived from the verse, "Therefore a man shall leave his father," meaning his father's wife, "and his mother," literally; "and shall cleave," excluding a male; "to his wife," excluding another man's wife; "and they shall become one flesh," excluding an animal. It is also stated, "She is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife." These are the words of R' Akiva in Sanhedrin, daf 55a. Yet according to R' Akiva his sister is permitted, as stated there on daf 55b; see Rashi there, s.v. "come and hear," etc. Rambam, however, rules like the Sages on daf 57b and like the Toras Kohanim according to R' Yishmael: "Every forbidden relation," etc. The text appears not to read "many," but rather: there are relations for which a Jewish beit din does not execute, etc., namely those explained in the continuation, including his sister and a betrothed maiden. The matter of a betrothed maiden requires study. His sister is derived from "Therefore he shall leave," etc. According to R' Akiva the verse must be read less literally, while the Sages interpret it according to its plain meaning. In Toras Kohanim, Parashas Kedoshim, it is taught regarding "it is a disgraceful act": perhaps you will say that Kayin married his sister; Scripture therefore calls it an act of kindness, for at the beginning of the world it was permitted only because the world could not otherwise be established. This accords with Sanhedrin, daf 55b, "Come and hear, why," etc., and not with the Gemara's rejection there, nor with Rashi's explanation on daf 57b. Ramban likewise writes this, except that he holds that according to the Sages all maternal relatives are forbidden. The only dispute between Ramban and Rambam is therefore concerning the mother's sister through the mother, as explained by Ramban. There are twenty-two forbidden relations in all: four not based on kinship, namely a male, an animal, a married woman, and a niddah. All apply to a non-Jew except niddah. Eighteen are based on kinship, corresponding to the fifteen women and six forbidden relations listed in the first chapter of Yevamos, with the wife of one's brother counted in three forms and one's sister in two forms. Seven are one's own relatives, seven are relatives through one's wife, and four are wives of relatives whose husbands create the prohibition. For a ben Noach, the seven relatives through one's wife are all permitted because marital kinship does not create such relationships for non-Jews. Likewise, the four wives of relatives are all permitted except the father's wife, which R' Akiva derives from the verse, whereas according to R' Eliezer all are permitted. Of the seven direct blood relatives, those related through the father are all permitted, as stated in Yevamos, chapter 11, daf 98a, because a non-Jew has no halachic paternal relationship. Therefore the Gemara on daf 58b states that a non-Jew may marry his daughter, and all the more so his son's daughter and daughter's daughter. The same applies to the father's sister according to R' Akiva, whereas R' Eliezer derives a prohibition from the verse. Ramban nevertheless holds that the mother's sister is forbidden even according to R' Akiva, because the word "saying" extends the prohibition to maternal relatives. Rambam, however, holds that even according to the Sages only the mother and maternal sister, which are explicitly stated, are forbidden, as in the view of R' Meir according to R' Akiva. R' Meir and the Sages disagree only concerning his sister and the interpretation of the verse. The Gemara on daf 57b asks, "Does R' Meir hold," etc. Ramban explains that the question concerns only the latter clause, which says that a ben Noach is not warned, etc., while here the Baraisa includes his sister. It does not ask from the father's wife because the Sages did not decree other paternal relatives upon converts. This differs from Rashi's explanation there. Proof is that the Gemara challenges specifically according to R' Meir; according to Rashi the same difficulty would apply to the Sages, who do not disagree on that point. It answers that one source follows R' Meir, etc., and the Baraisa likewise cannot accord with the Sages except concerning the sister. In the dispute of R' Eliezer ben Yaakov and R' Shimon in Yevamos, daf 97b, Rambam rules like Rav Acha bar Yaakov and the first version, unlike the Rif. His reason is the statement on daf 98a: "This that the Sages said," etc., which implies that even rabbinically a convert has no paternal relationship. The Gemara says that twin brothers, etc., and therefore any kinship containing a paternal side is permitted l'chatchila: the father's sister through the mother, the mother's sister through the father, and a paternal sister. Although the Baraisa there forbids all of these, it has already been established according to R' Eliezer, who holds the father's sister is forbidden to a ben Noach. According to R' Akiva and the Sages, any relation containing a paternal side is entirely permitted. Ramban and Rashba likewise write this. A mother's sister through the mother, however, is rabbinically forbidden to a convert even though she is permitted to a ben Noach, because the Gemara's statement that a non-Jew has no father implies that maternal kinship does exist. The same applies to maternal brothers. Likewise, a paternal relationship created through marriage is permitted, even the father's wife according to all opinions, except for the wife of his maternal brother, as explained. The Gemara's statement, "What, is it not," etc., concerns only the wife of his brother, unlike the Ra'avad's explanation that it applies to all relations created through marriage. For the Gemara also counts the wife of his father's brother, who is certainly permitted even if that marriage occurred after conversion. Ramban. There is an additional distinction between the Baraisa and the Sages: according to the Baraisa, the mother's sister through the mother must be divorced, whereas according to the Sages he may retain her, like the father's sister through the father according to R' Meir, because the prohibition is only to prevent confusion. The same applies to the mother's sister through the mother according to R' Akiva and the Sages, and all the more so to the wife of his maternal brother. This is Rambam's approach, and this is the meaning of his words, "If he was married," etc., regarding the other relations, etc.

(Likkut) See what is written there. The general rule according to Rambam is as follows: for a ben Noach, his mother, maternal sister, and father's wife are forbidden, while all other relatives are entirely permitted, in accordance with the Sages who disagree with R' Meir. For a convert, paternal relationships are entirely permitted, whether direct blood relatives or relatives through marriage. He may therefore even marry his father's former wife, and in this respect a convert is more lenient than a non-Jew. On the other hand, every maternal relationship is forbidden to a convert, whether through direct blood relationship or through marriage. Thus, among his own relatives he is forbidden to his mother and his mother's sister through the mother. Among his wife's relatives he is forbidden to his wife's maternal sister, his wife's daughter and granddaughter, his mother-in-law, and his wife's maternal grandmother, as written in seif 5, "one who marries," etc.; the same applies to the corresponding cases, as Tosafos and Ramban write. Through marriage he is also forbidden to the wife of his maternal brother. These are nine forbidden relations in all. Ramban's approach regarding a convert agrees with Rambam, but regarding a non-Jew he holds that according to all opinions all maternal relatives are forbidden and all paternal relatives are permitted. Relations created through marriage do not apply at all except those explicitly specified: the father's sister through the mother according to R' Eliezer, and the father's wife according to R' Akiva. According to R' Meir in accordance with R' Akiva, only maternal relations punishable by death are forbidden, whereas according to R' Eliezer and the Sages even those punishable by karet are forbidden. Rashi has another approach; see Ramban's discussion. End.

corrected_en: Once he struck it with one blow of a hoe, he acquires the whole. I was uncertain whether one who takes possession of the property of a deceased convert, with movable property located within it, acquires those movables through kinyan agav. Perhaps kinyan agav works only where there is another person transferring ownership, whereas one who acquires on his own cannot acquire through agav. The practical difference is where the law of courtyard acquisition does not apply, such as where the courtyard is not guarded and he neither stands beside it nor says, "My field shall acquire for me." At first glance there is proof from the fact that houses are acquired by chazakah in the property of a deceased convert, as indicated in Bava Basra, daf 53, concerning two houses, one inside the other. According to the poskim who hold that a house has the status of something detached and subsequently attached, so that its law is like movable property, as explained in siman 95, and as I wrote there in seif katan 3 in the name of Magen Avraham, siman 637, the acquisition of houses there would necessarily be through agav. This would prove that ownerless property can also be acquired through agav. One can nevertheless answer that the house is acquired through the law of a courtyard, because by acquiring the land beneath it through chazakah he simultaneously acquires the house through his courtyard, in accordance with what I wrote in siman 202 that acquisition of the courtyard and the object given can take effect simultaneously.

There is, however, a clear proof that one can acquire ownerless property on his own through agav from the discussion in Bava Kamma, daf 117, regarding the dispute between R' Eliezer and the Sages concerning one who stole land and a river swept it away, whether land is subject to theft. The Baraisa states: one who steals a cow and it is swept away by a river must provide another cow, according to R' Eliezer, whereas the Sages say he may say, "Your property is before you." Rav Pappa explains that the case is where one stole another person's field while a cow was lying in it, and the river swept it away. R' Eliezer follows his view and the Sages follow theirs. Rashi explains that the cow was lying there and the robber did not perform meshichah upon it. According to R' Eliezer, who holds that the field is acquired by the robber, the cow is acquired together with it and he is liable to pay, because movable property is acquired agav land. According to the Sages, he acquires neither the field nor the cow. In the case of a robber there is no other person consciously transferring ownership. Yet the robber requires a kinyan in order to become liable for unavoidable loss just as one requires a kinyan to acquire ownership, and Rashi says that he acquires through agav. This proves that kinyan agav operates even where one acquires without another transferor, as with ownerless property. Rashi did not explain that he acquires the cow through courtyard acquisition, for a courtyard acquires because it is a person's legal domain, whereas a robber acquires land only with respect to liability for unavoidable loss and has no proprietary right in the courtyard itself. Although with all objects subject to theft he pays according to the value at the time of theft and need not pay for his use of them, as explained in Shulchan Aruch, siman 363, and Rama, siman 371, that does not make the unlawfully occupied courtyard his domain. He entered it without permission. Therefore Rashi explained the acquisition as agav rather than courtyard acquisition. It is thus clearly proven that agav works for the property of a deceased convert.

There is nevertheless a distinction between ownerless property and property received as a gift. Regarding a gift we rule that agav does not require the movable property to be physically gathered upon the land, as explained in Shulchan Aruch, siman 202. Regarding ownerless property, however, it certainly must be physically gathered there. If one takes possession of the property of a deceased convert, he obviously cannot thereby acquire through agav every ownerless object in the world. The reason appears to be that ordinary agav requires the giver to say, "Acquire it together with the land." With ownerless property there is no giver who can say this. Even if the acquirer himself says, "I wish to acquire it together with the land," that statement is ineffective, because the formula "go and acquire together with the land" requires another person transferring ownership. Where the movables are physically gathered upon the land, however, the formula is unnecessary, as Rambam writes in chapter 3 of Hilchos Mechirah and as Shulchan Aruch rules in siman 202, seif 2. Maggid Mishneh explains that the Gemara's statement that agav does not require the movables to be gathered refers to where the giver says, "Go and acquire together with the land"; without such a statement, they must be physically gathered there. Since items physically within the land are regarded like the land itself, as Sema writes in siman 202, this also works for ownerless property: by acquiring the land, he acquires the movables that are gathered within it. This also explains why the Gemara in Bava Kamma specifically says that the cow was lying in the field. If agav never required physical presence, that detail would be unnecessary. Because there is no other transferor to say, "Go and acquire together with the land," the cow must be physically present. This supports Rambam's rule, even though Maggid Mishneh, Ran, and the Rosh question his distinction.

According to this, however, there is a difficulty from Bava Metzia, daf 11. The Gemara states that courtyard acquisition requires the owner to stand beside his field. R' Abba challenged Ulla from the incident involving Rabban Gamliel and the elders, where Rabban Gamliel said: "The tithe that I will measure is given to Yehoshua, and its place is rented to him," etc. R' Yehoshua and R' Akiva were not standing beside Rabban Gamliel's field. Ulla answered that Rabban Gamliel transferred the movable property to them through agav. R' Zeira accepted this, but R' Abba did not. Rava said that R' Abba was correct not to accept it: did they not have a sudar through which to acquire by chalipin? Rather, the benefit of choosing to whom to give the tithes is not money for purposes of acquisition by chalipin; likewise, it is not money for purposes of acquisition through agav. Rashi explains that this right is not property belonging to Rabban Gamliel. He merely made the produce ownerless toward them, and when he rented its location to them, their courtyards acquired it as with other ownerless property.

According to what I wrote, that ownerless property can be acquired through agav when it is physically gathered upon the land, what is Rava's question from chalipin? Chalipin certainly does not work because the right to choose the recipient is not money and therefore is not the owner's property to transfer. But agav should work perfectly well, because after it becomes ownerless the recipients could acquire it themselves through agav, just as they could acquire ownerless property through a courtyard.

It appears that this can be answered according to the Shitah Mekubetzes there, which writes concerning the statement that the benefit of choosing the recipient is not money: even if one holds that it is money, it is not sufficiently significant money to be acquired through chalipin. Thus the sugya can accord both with the view that this right is not money and with the view that it is money. Although it cannot be acquired through chalipin or agav because those are weak forms of kinyan, if one person gave another a maneh and transferred to him the right to choose the recipient of these fruits, he would acquire it. Otherwise the Gemara should simply have said that the right is not money and cannot be acquired. By saying that it is "not money to acquire through chalipin," it implies that in some forms it can indeed be acquired. These words are compelled, because Rava explicitly holds in Nedarim, daf 85, that the benefit of choosing the recipient is money. Rather, Rava means that even though it is money, it is too slight a monetary right to be acquired through the weak kinyanim of chalipin and agav. I was uncertain whether one who takes possession of the property of a deceased convert, with movable property located within it, acquires those movables through kinyan agav. Perhaps kinyan agav works only where there is another person transferring ownership, whereas one who acquires on his own cannot acquire through agav. The practical difference is where the law of courtyard acquisition does not apply, such as where the courtyard is not guarded and he neither stands beside it nor says, "My field shall acquire for me." At first glance there is proof from the fact that houses are acquired by chazakah in the property of a deceased convert, as indicated in Bava Basra, daf 53, concerning two houses, one inside the other. According to the poskim who hold that a house has the status of something detached and subsequently attached, so that its law is like movable property, as explained in siman 95, and as I wrote there in seif katan 3 in the name of Magen Avraham, siman 637, the acquisition of houses there would necessarily be through agav. This would prove that ownerless property can also be acquired through agav. One can nevertheless answer that the house is acquired through the law of a courtyard, because by acquiring the land beneath it through chazakah he simultaneously acquires the house through his courtyard, in accordance with what I wrote in siman 202 that acquisition of the courtyard and the object given can take effect simultaneously.

There is, however, a clear proof that one can acquire ownerless property on his own through agav from the discussion in Bava Kamma, daf 117, regarding the dispute between R' Eliezer and the Sages concerning one who stole land and a river swept it away, whether land is subject to theft. The Baraisa states: one who steals a cow and it is swept away by a river must provide another cow, according to R' Eliezer, whereas the Sages say he may say, "Your property is before you." Rav Pappa explains that the case is where one stole another person's field while a cow was lying in it, and the river swept it away. R' Eliezer follows his view and the Sages follow theirs. Rashi explains that the cow was lying there and the robber did not perform meshichah upon it. According to R' Eliezer, who holds that the field is acquired by the robber, the cow is acquired together with it and he is liable to pay, because movable property is acquired agav land. According to the Sages, he acquires neither the field nor the cow. In the case of a robber there is no other person consciously transferring ownership. Yet the robber requires a kinyan in order to become liable for unavoidable loss just as one requires a kinyan to acquire ownership, and Rashi says that he acquires through agav. This proves that kinyan agav operates even where one acquires without another transferor, as with ownerless property. Rashi did not explain that he acquires the cow through courtyard acquisition, for a courtyard acquires because it is a person's legal domain, whereas a robber acquires land only with respect to liability for unavoidable loss and has no proprietary right in the courtyard itself. Although with all objects subject to theft he pays according to the value at the time of theft and need not pay for his use of them, as explained in Shulchan Aruch, siman 363, and Rama, siman 371, that does not make the unlawfully occupied courtyard his domain. He entered it without permission. Therefore Rashi explained the acquisition as agav rather than courtyard acquisition. It is thus clearly proven that agav works for the property of a deceased convert.

There is nevertheless a distinction between ownerless property and property received as a gift. Regarding a gift we rule that agav does not require the movable property to be physically gathered upon the land, as explained in Shulchan Aruch, siman 202. Regarding ownerless property, however, it certainly must be physically gathered there. If one takes possession of the property of a deceased convert, he obviously cannot thereby acquire through agav every ownerless object in the world. The reason appears to be that ordinary agav requires the giver to say, "Acquire it together with the land." With ownerless property there is no giver who can say this. Even if the acquirer himself says, "I wish to acquire it together with the land," that statement is ineffective, because the formula "go and acquire together with the land" requires another person transferring ownership. Where the movables are physically gathered upon the land, however, the formula is unnecessary, as Rambam writes in chapter 3 of Hilchos Mechirah and as Shulchan Aruch rules in siman 202, seif 2. Maggid Mishneh explains that the Gemara's statement that agav does not require the movables to be gathered refers to where the giver says, "Go and acquire together with the land"; without such a statement, they must be physically gathered there. Since items physically within the land are regarded like the land itself, as Sema writes in siman 202, this also works for ownerless property: by acquiring the land, he acquires the movables that are gathered within it. This also explains why the Gemara in Bava Kamma specifically says that the cow was lying in the field. If agav never required physical presence, that detail would be unnecessary. Because there is no other transferor to say, "Go and acquire together with the land," the cow must be physically present. This supports Rambam's rule, even though Maggid Mishneh, Ran, and the Rosh question his distinction.
